newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks off on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks off on profit-taking.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks drifted lower Wednesday as investors cashed in profits one day after the Dow Jones industrial average closed above the 6,600-point level for the first time.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow was off 10.01 points at 6,590.65, retreating from Tuesday's record of 6,600.66.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 13-9 on active volume of 316 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite was up 0.16 of a point at 1,327.89. The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.58 at 577.21.
Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co. said the New Year's influx of pension fund money, which has boosted stocks recently, was showing signs of slowing.
He said the market's sluggishness indicated that it was at "the tail end of the Santa Claus rally, and pretty soon the markets will be in a marked sell-off."

According to the seasonal pattern, stocks gain in December in what is known as the Santa Claus rally as pressure from end-of-year selling for tax or other reasons, tapers off. The rally extends into the New Year as cash flows into mutual funds from corporated bonus payments, dividend distributions and annual retirement account contributions.
Barthel said the recent rebound in long-term interest rates also was capping the rally in stocks.
"Rates are higher than they were 30 days ago and that is usually a precursor to a downturn in stocks," he said.
The yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was at 6.78 percent, up from 6.33 about a month ago.
Analysts said the stock market shrugged off comments by New York Federal Reserve President William McDonough that stocks were fairly valued.
"I don't think his saying that has any bearing on the market," said Richard Cripps, market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker in Baltimore.

In a speech in New York City, McDonough, who is vice chairman of the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee, which sets the nation's interest rates, said, "I have no idea," when asked if he thought the stock market was overvalued.
"Does it seem to be rather fully valued?," he asked. "By all conventional measures, yes."

McDonough's comments come just a month after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan sent stocks reeling with his remarks about the "irrational exuberance" of financial markets, which suggested that the central bank might raise interest rates to cool the the upward drive in stocks.
Among active stocks, Motorola Inc. rose 1-3/4 to 63-1/2 after Morgan Stanley raised its rating on the company.
Ford Motor Co. rose 3/4 to 34-1/4 after the carmaker said it was weighing the sale of its Budget rental car unit.
Shiva Corp. plummeted 15-1/4, or 44 percent, to 19-1/2 after the data communications equipment company said its fourth quarter earnings would be well below Wall Street consensus estimates.
